race_context: The 'Jefferson Madison' races on the state list are for the Board of School Trustees of Madison Consolidated Schools (MCS), based in Madison in Jefferson County; the superintendent is Dr. Teresa Brown {mcs_board}{mcs_team}. State enrollment counts were 2,554 students in 2023-24, 2,651 in 2024-25 and 2,672 in 2025-26 {idoe_enroll}. In August 2026 Brown told the board MCS had 2,600 students, up 65 from the year before {mc_enroll}.

The board has five members: David Storie (president), Dustin Bentz (vice president), Jodi Yancey (secretary), Michael Scott and John Wallace {mcs_board}{mcs_jan14}. Seats are tied to residence districts: District 1 (Madison precincts 1, 2 and 3 and Graham, Lancaster, Milton, Monroe and Shelby townships) has two members, District 2 (precincts 4-1, 4-1A, 4-2, 4-3, 5-1 and 5-2) has two, and District 3 (precincts 1-1, 1-2, 2-1, 2-2 and the 3rd ward) has one {mc_2024_filing}{mc_bentz}{mc_filing_open}.

Seats on the 2026 ballot: two District 2 seats and one District 3 seat {mc_filing_open}{mc_filing_begins}. The state list shows District 2 as 'vote for 1', but the Madison Courier reports District 2 'is for two positions'; in 2022 the District 2 race was also 'choose two' {in_list}{mc_races_set}{mc_2022_totals}. District 2 members Jodi Yancey (first elected 2018) and John Wallace (elected 2022) chose not to run again, so Anthony Miller and Jacqueline Overpeck, the only two District 2 candidates, would fill both seats {mc_races_set}{mc_filing_begins}. District 3 member Michael Scott (elected unopposed in 2022) is running for a second term against Jill Kelly-Koren {mc_races_set}{mc_2022_forum}.

Party labels: the state list shows Kelly-Koren as Democratic and Miller, Overpeck and Scott as Nonpartisan {in_list}. Filing ran from May 19 to a June 18 noon deadline, which was extended to noon June 22, 2026 after a storm knocked out power at the Jefferson County Courthouse; Miller, Overpeck and Kelly-Koren all filed in the final days {mc_filing_open}{mc_outage}{mc_races_set}.

Budget and SEA 1: at a Sept. 9, 2026 hearing MCS advertised a 2027 budget of $41,601,979 ($25.0 million education fund, $10.9 million operations, $5.7 million debt service) and a tax rate of $1.1942; chief financial officer Danica Houze said the rate will go up because of Senate Bill 1, so the district can keep its levy as assessed values change {mc_budget}. The board is scheduled to adopt the budget Oct. 14 {mc_budget}.

Early Learning Center (2025-2026): in January 2026 the district's building corporation approved $22 million in bonds, part of $28 million in total borrowing, to build an Early Learning Center on the site of the closed E.O. Muncie Elementary, and the board awarded a $353,000 demolition contract {mc_elc}. The district's municipal adviser said the new bonds will be repaid through 2045 {mc_elc}.

Teacher pay: in November 2025 the board ratified a teacher contract that raised the salary schedule by $1,500 across the board plus a step for returning teachers; then-president Wallace credited the raises to the superintendent's team, 'the cuts made and the increased enrollment' {mcs_nov5}. Teacher contract talks with the Madison Teachers Association begin again this fall {mc_enroll}.

Programs and choice: in July 2026 the board created the Jefferson County Virtual Academy for grades 6-12, open to students outside the district, and approved rejoining the Southeast Career Center, where Brown said 45 to 50 high school students had registered {mc_virtual}. A state-mandated cell phone policy bars student phone use from the start of the school day until dismissal {mc_enroll}.
Forums: this guide found no 2026 candidate forum or questionnaire for these races, and no candidate websites. The only campaign coverage found was the Madison Courier's filing reports {mc_races_set}.

review_flags.summary: At an Oct. 28, 2024 special meeting, then-board president John Wallace said Scott had violated the board's code of ethics policy by endorsing two candidates in the 2024 District 1 race during the board's Oct. 2, 2024 meeting. Scott read an apology, said 'My opinion wasn't needed and I violated our Code of Ethics Policy,' gave up his $500 fourth-quarter stipend and asked to be replaced as vice president; David Storie was elected vice president for the rest of 2024 {mc_ethics}{mc_ratify_2024}.
review_flags.note: Self-imposed penalties after the board president cited a policy violation; no formal censure vote was reported. Scott remains a board member and is seeking reelection.
